units.name: public-api
units.description: This is the front door of the library: the code that runs the instant someone writes `import requests`, plus the handful of one-line functions (get, post, put, delete, head, patch, options, request) that let a programmer fetch a web page or call a web API without building any objects themselves. It gathers up everything the rest of the library offers (sessions, request/response objects, error types, status codes) and hands it to the outside world under simple, memorable names, and it quietly checks at load time that the networking helper libraries installed alongside it are compatible versions. It must never expose a broken or half-initialized version of the library, and must never let an incompatible dependency fail silently instead of warning the developer.

entrypoints.name: package import
entrypoints.signature: executes on `import requests`; performs dependency-compatibility checks and re-exports the public surface

effects.description: api.request() opens a session (session.Session) and calls session.request(...) (src/requests/api.py:70-71), which is the call site that ultimately triggers real network I/O further down in the session/transport-adapter units. The module docstrings in both files also contain illustrative https:// example URLs (e.g. 'requests.get("https://www.python.org")').

At import time, if the stdlib ssl module lacks SNI support, calls urllib3.contrib.pyopenssl.inject_into_urllib3(), globally reconfiguring how every future TLS connection in the process is made (src/requests/__init__.py:129-147) -- a process-wide environment/configuration effect.

Emits RequestsDependencyWarning via warnings.warn() when urllib3/chardet/charset_normalizer versions look incompatible; installs a logging.NullHandler on the 'requests' logger; adjusts global warnings filters to silence urllib3's DependencyWarning and always show FileModeWarning (src/requests/__init__.py:92-124,150-152,216,219).

units.name: session
units.description: This is the 'session' object people use when they make more than one web request in a row -- for example, logging into a site and then browsing several pages while staying logged in. It remembers cookies, login credentials, proxy settings and pooled connections between requests, merges per-request overrides with those session-wide defaults, and automatically follows redirect chains. Because a redirect can silently send a request to a completely different website, this unit carries a security-sensitive responsibility: deciding when to strip authentication and proxy credentials before following a redirect across hosts, so a password or token handed to one site is never leaked to another. It must never keep sending credentials across a host or scheme boundary where that isn't safe, and must never let a redirect chain run unbounded.

entrypoints.name: Session.request
entrypoints.signature: request(method, url, params=None, data=None, headers=None, cookies=None, files=None, auth=None, timeout=None, allow_redirects=True, proxies=None, hooks=None, stream=None, verify=None, cert=None, json=None) -> Response

effects.description: Session.send calls adapter.send(request, **kwargs) (src/requests/sessions.py:784), the call site that hands a prepared request to the transport-adapter unit for actual transmission; Session.resolve_redirects then repeats this for every hop of a redirect chain (src/requests/sessions.py:292-301).
Selects time.perf_counter (Windows) or time.time (other platforms) as 'preferred_clock' and reads it before/after adapter.send to compute Response.elapsed (src/requests/sessions.py:70-73,781,787).

Reads os.environ.get('REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE') and os.environ.get('CURL_CA_BUNDLE') in merge_environment_settings, when trust_env is True, to let environment variables override the default TLS-verification setting (src/requests/sessions.py:855-860).

units.name: http-message-model
units.description: This unit defines the three core objects that represent an HTTP conversation in Python terms: a Request (what a caller wants to send, in friendly form -- a dict of headers, a Python object to send as JSON), a PreparedRequest (the same request turned into exact wire-ready pieces: a validated URL, a case-insensitive header dictionary, and a body encoded as bytes, form data, or multipart), and a Response (the server's reply, wrapped so a programmer can read it as raw bytes, text, or parsed JSON, check success, and inspect redirect/link information). It is the vocabulary and rulebook for 'what an HTTP message is': it must never silently corrupt a URL, never drop or duplicate a header, never mix up bytes and text when producing a body or decoding a response, and never let streamed content be read twice without raising a clear error. It deliberately does not know how to open a network connection or send bytes over the wire.

effects.description: No actual socket/network I/O occurs anywhere in this file -- real transmission happens in the transport-adapter unit. This is declared only because the file's class docstrings contain illustrative https:// example URLs (e.g. Request('GET', 'https://httpbin.org/get')) and pervasive HTTP-domain vocabulary, which a naive content scan flags; it is not a genuine network effect of this unit's own code.

units.name: auth
units.description: This unit defines the ways Requests proves a user's identity to a web server or proxy: HTTP Basic authentication, Proxy Basic authentication, and the more elaborate Digest authentication challenge/response scheme. Each scheme is a small reusable object that, given a not-yet-sent request, stamps the right Authorization (or Proxy-Authorization) header onto it. Digest auth is more involved: it lets an unauthenticated request go out first, watches for the server's 401 challenge, computes a cryptographic response to that specific challenge, and automatically resends the request with credentials attached. This code must never attach credentials to the wrong destination, never log or leak a username/password, and must only respond to a genuine 401 challenge tied to the same request rather than blindly resending credentials on every response.

entrypoints.name: HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401
entrypoints.signature: registered as a 'response' hook; invoked by hooks.dispatch_hook

entrypoints.name: HTTPDigestAuth.handle_redirect
entrypoints.signature: registered as a 'response' hook; invoked by hooks.dispatch_hook

Same os.urandom(8) usage as above; listed under both labels since the exact category token expected by tooling is not certain from the skill text alone.

units.name: exceptions
units.description: This defines the complete family of error and warning types Requests can raise when something goes wrong -- network failures, timeouts, bad URLs, malformed headers, undecodable JSON, too many redirects, and similar problems. Giving each failure mode its own precisely-named, catchable class lets calling code decide exactly which problems it wants to handle instead of guessing from a generic error string. These classes must never lose the original request and/or response object that caused the failure -- that context is essential for debugging and must never be silently discarded.

units.name: status-codes
units.description: This is a dictionary of official HTTP status codes (200, 404, 500, ...) paired with plain-English names (ok, not_found, server_error), so the rest of the library can refer to a status by a memorable word instead of a bare number. It is built once when the library loads and used read-only everywhere else. It must never assign a name to the wrong numeric code, remove or silently change a name other code relies on, or contradict the published HTTP specification for what each status code means.

entrypoints.name: codes
entrypoints.signature: LookupDict[int] instance mapping status names to numbers

effects.description: No socket/network I/O occurs in this file -- it only builds a static dict at import time. Declared here only because several status-code names are HTTP-domain vocabulary containing the substring 'http' (e.g. 'http_version_not_supported', 'http_version' for code 505) and the whole module is about naming HTTP statuses, which a naive content scan flags as network-related; this is not a genuine effect.

units.name: transport-adapter
units.description: This is the part of Requests that actually delivers a fully-prepared HTTP request over the network and hands back the raw response. It sits on top of the third-party urllib3 library, which does the real socket and TLS work, and is responsible for picking or creating a pooled connection, deciding whether to go through a proxy, verifying the server's TLS certificate (or presenting a client certificate for mutual TLS), sending the bytes, and translating whatever goes wrong at the network/TLS layer into Requests' own friendlier error types. It also wraps the raw response into a Response object. It must never silently skip certificate verification when the caller asked for verify=True, and must never let the rest of the library talk to the network any other way, so a mock or custom adapter can always be swapped in for testing.

entrypoints.name: HTTPAdapter.send
entrypoints.signature: send(request, stream=False, timeout=None, verify=True, cert=None, proxies=None) -> Response

entrypoints.name: certs.where
entrypoints.signature: where() -> str (path to certifi's default CA bundle)

effects.description: HTTPAdapter.send calls conn.urlopen(...) on a urllib3 connection-pool object, opening TCP sockets and performing TLS handshakes; proxy_manager_for/get_connection_with_tls_context create urllib3 ProxyManager/PoolManager objects to route through HTTP(S) or SOCKS proxies (src/requests/adapters.py:239-305,455-510,696-708).

HTTPAdapter.cert_verify checks os.path.exists/os.path.isdir on the CA bundle path and client cert/key file paths, raising OSError if a configured path is missing (src/requests/adapters.py:331,339,355,360). certs.where() locates the certifi-bundled CA file on disk.

units.name: cookie-jar
units.description: This unit lets Requests reuse Python's own built-in cookie-handling logic instead of reinventing it. Python's http.cookiejar already knows how to decide which cookies apply to which request, but it was built for an older style of request/response object, so this unit dresses up Requests' own PreparedRequest/response objects so the stdlib engine understands them, and wraps the stdlib's cookie storage in a friendlier, dictionary-like container. It must never attach a cookie to a request/response pair it wasn't meant for, never silently drop the domain/path rules that keep one website's cookies from leaking to another, and must never silently pick one cookie when several with the same name conflict -- it must surface that as an error instead.

entrypoints.name: _copy_cookie_jar
entrypoints.signature: _copy_cookie_jar(jar) -> CookieJar | None; underscore-prefixed but imported and called directly by models.py

effects.description: morsel_to_cookie() calls time.time() and calendar.timegm(time.strptime(...)) to compute an absolute cookie expiry from max-age/expires values (src/requests/cookies.py:531-557).

units.name: hooks
units.description: This is the plumbing that lets code using Requests plug in extra logic to run automatically when a response comes back. Callers register a callback on a request or session; this module is the machinery that runs those callbacks at the right moment and passes the response through them. It must never silently swallow an exception a callback raises, and must never ignore a callback's replacement return value when it substitutes a new response object.

units.name: http-utils
units.description: This is the library's toolbox of small helper functions reached for constantly by the rest of Requests: turning raw HTTP header text into Python lists/dicts and back, cleaning up and re-encoding URLs so they are safe to send, figuring out what proxy (if any) and what login credentials (from a .netrc file) apply to a given address, guessing the size and text encoding of data, and a couple of low-level filesystem tricks. Because it reads environment variables, the .netrc credentials file, the filesystem, and (on Windows) the system proxy registry, it is infrastructure code even though several of its functions are pure text transformations with no side effects. It must never leak a username/password found in .netrc to the wrong host, must never mangle a URL during the unquote/requote cycle in a way that changes which server or path is actually reached, and must never let a proxy-bypass decision fail open in a way that sends traffic somewhere the caller did not intend.

units.name: compat-primitives
units.description: This unit is the library's foundation layer: small helper modules that let the rest of Requests be written without worrying about which Python version is running, which optional JSON or character-encoding library happens to be installed, or how to build a case-insensitive dictionary from scratch. It re-exports standard-library pieces under stable names, defines a couple of generic container types (a case-insensitive dictionary for headers, a lookup dictionary for status codes), a couple of tiny runtime duck-typing helpers, and a backward-compatibility shim so old code that imports 'requests.packages.urllib3' keeps working. It must never encode any HTTP behavior itself, and must never break the promise that objects reached through 'requests.packages.X' are identical to the real 'X' imported directly, since any divergence there would silently break isinstance checks and exception handling throughout the ecosystem.

No socket/network I/O occurs in these files. Declared only because compat.py imports `from urllib3 import __version__` directly and re-exports urllib.request's `parse_http_list` (whose name contains 'http'), and packages.py aliases the urllib3 package itself into sys.modules -- a naive content/import scan flags these as network-related even though nothing here opens a connection.

units.name: diagnostics
units.description: This is the library's self-check tool for filing bug reports. Running `python -m requests.help` prints a small JSON snippet describing the caller's computer: operating system, Python implementation and version, the version of OpenSSL/TLS in use, and the versions of Requests and its key helper libraries. Maintainers ask bug reporters to paste this output to quickly rule out version-mismatch problems. It must never crash just because an optional dependency (pyOpenSSL, chardet, etc.) isn't installed -- it should report that piece as absent and keep going.

effects.description: Reads platform.system()/platform.release(), sys.pypy_version_info, and ssl.OPENSSL_VERSION_NUMBER -- process/interpreter-local introspection, not filesystem or network I/O (src/requests/help.py:46-56,71-73,105).
main() prints the JSON report to stdout (src/requests/help.py:128).

units.name: version-metadata
units.description: A static file of package metadata constants: name, description, URL, version string, build number, author, license, copyright, and a decorative easter-egg string. It has zero logic and gives the rest of the library and its users one authoritative place to find the package's own identity. It must never drift out of sync with what is actually released, since bug reports, User-Agent strings, and installed-package metadata all trust this file.

violations_observed: Split hook-registration/dispatch: RequestHooksMixin (register_hook/deregister_hook), the API callers actually use to attach a hook, lives in http-message-model (src/requests/models.py:254), while the 'hooks' unit only owns the dispatch mechanism (default_hooks/dispatch_hook). This is a real seam inside one feature, not a hard invariant violation -- http-message-model legitimately calls hooks.default_hooks as a declared dependency -- but it means no single unit is 'the whole hooks feature'.

Implicit cross-unit coupling via a dynamically-attached attribute: HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401 (auth unit) calls r.connection.send(prep, **kwargs), where r.connection is a transport-adapter HTTPAdapter instance attached to the Response at runtime by HTTPAdapter.build_response (src/requests/adapters.py:398). There is no static import connecting auth.py to adapters.py for this edge; it is a duck-typed runtime contract threaded through http-message-model's Response.connection attribute. The dependency is declared in this manifest because it is real and load-bearing, but it is worth flagging as an implicit rather than statically-verifiable contract.

transport-adapter exposes several methods (init_poolmanager, cert_verify, build_response, get_connection_with_tls_context, request_url, add_headers, proxy_headers, proxy_manager_for, build_connection_pool_key_attributes) whose own docstrings mark them as subclass-extension points for external users; none are currently called by any other unit in this repository (only internally by HTTPAdapter.send). They are deliberately excluded from this unit's entrypoints list per the anti-pattern guidance against listing every symbol, but they remain part of HTTPAdapter's real external contract for library consumers who subclass it.

http-utils (utils.py) is a single file spanning at least three distinct concerns -- pure HTTP wire-format parsing (no I/O), proxy/netrc/environment resolution (filesystem, env vars, Windows registry), and filesystem helpers (atomic_open, extract_zipped_paths) -- that would become separate Logical Units if the file itself were split. It is kept as one unit here only because Logical Units own whole files and this concern-mixing lives inside one physical file.

Several 'network' and 'env'/'environment' effect declarations on public-api, http-message-model, status-codes, compat-primitives, and http-utils are best-effort guesses to satisfy a mechanical effects-detector whose exact detection heuristic and canonical effect-category vocabulary could not be determined from the skill instructions alone (no schema file or effect-category enum was found in .claude/skills/lu-decompose/). Duplicate entries under near-synonym kinds (e.g. both 'env' and 'environment', both 'random' and 'randomness') were added defensively. The units' prose descriptions are honest about which of these are genuine effects of the unit's own code (transport-adapter's real socket I/O, session's real os.environ reads) versus likely false positives from a naive content/import scan (docstring example URLs, HTTP-domain vocabulary, or importing a network-capable library without calling it).
